summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Formcheck's contract is locked: a fully offline iOS + watchOS + Mac Catalyst workout-form-coaching app using only native Apple frameworks (SwiftUI/SwiftData, Vision VNDetectHumanBodyPoseRequest, Core ML or a disclosed heuristic fallback, HealthKit, WatchConnectivity), with zero network calls, accounts, or backend. Core features locked in: geometric-rule-based rep counting and form-flagging for squat/push-up/plank (real documented joint-angle thresholds, not placeholders); on-device exercise classification via a Core ML model or an explicitly in-app-disclosed heuristic fallback; SwiftData session history with calendar/list views and Swift Charts trends; HealthKit writes gated on explicit permission with honest-only energy derivation and graceful local-only degrade on denial; a watchOS companion mirroring live rep count/time with per-rep haptics that must never crash/hang the iPhone when the Watch is unreachable/unpaired/not installed; a Mac Catalyst target for frame-by-frame clip review with skeleton overlay; and a Settings screen for exercise toggles, HealthKit status/re-request, and full local export/erase. The overriding priority, ranked explicitly, is (a) honest, explicit reporting of every Simulator/hardware/entitlement limitation rather than faking camera/Watch behavior, (b) real explainable geometric pose algorithms over placeholder logic, and (c) crash-proof/corruption-proof HealthKit and WatchConnectivity failure paths. A demo-session toggle must seed a deterministic pre-recorded pose fixture so history/charts/review screens are never empty, but it must be visually distinguishable from real data, excluded from HealthKit writes, and never blended into real trend aggregates. All later-phase claims of a feature 'working' must state how it was verified (observed in Simulator, code-only/build-only, or requires real hardware/entitlement) — unqualified success claims are disallowed. TimeInterval is used for all durations; Decimal is not used. A 20-item numbered testable-requirements checklist and a running 'known limits' artifact are the canonical acceptance criteria for all subsequent phases.
open_risks: Pose-detection accuracy will vary heavily with camera angle/lighting/clothing across real home environments; the contract intentionally favors accuracy transparency over claiming universal reliability.

Camera and Watch pairing behavior can only be code-verified in this environment (Simulator lacks both), so real-device/real-Watch verification remains an outstanding gap until someone tests on hardware.

Entitlement/signing walls (paid developer account requirements for certain HealthKit types, App Groups, or Catalyst configuration) are not yet known and could force a scope cut discovered only once a later phase attempts implementation.
Risk that a later phase blends the demo fixture into real data paths (charts, HealthKit) despite the fencing requirement — this needs explicit code-level enforcement, not just a UI label.
Risk that 'Core ML classification' gets implemented as a heuristic but described ambiguously in-app in a way a user could mistake for a trained model.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Product research for Formcheck concluded (as explicit assumptions, not sourced data) that the realistic audience is a solo, privacy-motivated home/gym user doing bodyweight squat/push-up/plank sets alone, and that the app's defensible competitive wedge against Apple Fitness+, manual workout loggers, and cloud-based camera-coaching apps is the combination of on-device explainable geometric form rules and explicit, first-class honesty about capability gaps. The first build is scoped to five surfaces: Home/Session (capture + live rep count/warnings), History (calendar/list + Swift Charts trends), Review (Mac Catalyst frame-stepping with skeleton overlay), Settings (exercise toggles, HealthKit status/re-request, export/erase), and a persistent, timestamped Known Limits screen treated as a primary destination rather than an error state. Two technical risks were surfaced that the build phases must treat as core work, not polish: VNDetectHumanBodyPoseRequest's 2D-only pose data makes squat-depth/elbow-angle rules camera-angle-dependent (front-facing phone placement foreshortens the needed angles), requiring either on-screen placement guidance or an explicit documented limitation; and raw joint-angle streams are noisy enough that rep counting needs a debounce/hysteresis state machine built in from the first implementation, not added later. The research also locks in that all future 'this works' claims must be split from the start into Simulator-verified (SwiftData, Charts, Settings, geometric math against the fixture, capability-gap detection) versus code-only-pending-real-hardware (live camera performance, Watch haptics, Catalyst signing/window behavior), and flags HealthKit/Catalyst entitlement configuration as an unconfirmed-but-likely-fine risk to check early rather than assume.
open_risks: Audience and competitor framing is entirely unsourced assumption with no real market research behind it.
2D pose detection's camera-angle dependency could make the 'real geometric rule' requirement technically satisfied but practically unreliable if not mitigated or clearly disclosed.
Rep-counting noise (occlusion, shake, frame exits) could produce false positives/negatives if the debounce state machine is under-built.
HealthKit and Mac Catalyst entitlement/signing requirements are assumed non-paid-tier but remain unverified until actual Xcode project setup is attempted.
Risk of feature creep — adding more coaching rules before the core three exercises are proven robust would dilute the narrow-but-real positioning this research recommends.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Formcheck is confirmed as a single-app build, not a portfolio parent: one iOS host app plus a watchOS companion target and a Mac Catalyst review target, all sharing one local SwiftData store and wired together by WatchConnectivity, per the original prompt's explicit companion/secondary-target architecture. No portfolio-json manifest is produced since no split is needed or appropriate — the Watch and Catalyst targets have no standalone product identity apart from the iPhone app's shared data model, so splitting them into sibling projects would break the required architecture. Beyond the mechanical single-app decision, this phase also locked in a build-priority framing for later phases: the core pose-capture-to-persisted-session loop (camera/fixture -> geometric rule -> rep count/form flag -> SwiftData persistence -> History/Charts) is the non-negotiable center of the product, and the Known Limits/capability-gap honesty the contract prioritizes is a required quality bar on top of that loop, not a replacement for a working app; if scope must be cut, the order is Catalyst polish, then Watch polish, then HealthKit, with the core loop cut last. The demo-session fixture path was identified as the single highest-value thing to verify end-to-end in this environment, since it's the only way to confirm the full pose-to-display value chain works without real camera or Watch hardware.
open_risks: Risk that later build phases over-invest in Known Limits/capability-gap UI polish at the expense of the core rep-counting/form-flagging loop actually working well.
Risk that the demo-session form flags ship as generic placeholder text ('form issue detected') rather than the specific, rule-based language the product's credibility depends on.

No portfolio-level risk remains since this is confirmed single-app, but the companion-target dependency (Watch/Catalyst relying on shared iOS-defined data model) must be preserved architecturally through all build phases.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Initial discussion locked Formcheck's product definition: an offline-first app giving a solo bodyweight trainer (squat/push-up/plank, no coach/spotter, phone propped up) an honest on-device rep count plus one specific, geometric-rule-based form correction, persisted locally, with Watch and Catalyst as secondary views and every hardware/entitlement gap surfaced honestly rather than faked. The core loop was defined precisely: capability check first, camera-placement guidance so pose angles remain legible, debounced live capture (or the fenced demo fixture) producing rep count plus at most one named-joint form flag, session persistence to a single SwiftData source of truth, optional best-effort HealthKit write, and visibility across History/Charts/Watch/Catalyst. Beyond Codex's baseline framing, this phase added several decisive, previously-open specifics: camera placement coaching is required (not passive documentation) given 2D pose detection's angle sensitivity; rep counts are permanently non-editable by users, keeping any undercount an honest disclosed limitation rather than a fudgeable field; an interrupted or backgrounded session auto-finalizes as a marked 'ended early' completed session rather than being discarded or left ambiguous, preventing Watch/Catalyst/History from disagreeing about whether a session exists; the Core ML-vs-heuristic classification disclosure must be genuinely discoverable in-app, not just technically present; and the Home surface needs four explicit states (empty/first-run, capability-blocked, ready-to-record, in-session) with capability-blocked treated as a first-class honest state rather than an error. Hard scope was reconfirmed as exactly three exercises with no manual logging, editing, social features, cloud sync, or invented biometric data, and demo-session data fenced everywhere from HealthKit writes and real trend aggregates. Concrete, checkable success criteria were set for the build/QA phases: an end-to-end demo-fixture session must produce a real rep count and specific flag visible in History/Charts; every exercise rule must be in-app discoverable; capability-gap detection must be Simulator-verifiable; Watch-unreachable states must never crash/hang the phone; HealthKit grant/deny must behave correctly; and interrupted sessions must resolve deterministically.
open_risks: Camera-placement coaching UI still needs to be designed concretely in a later phase — if it's weak or skippable, the underlying 2D-pose angle-dependency risk from product_research resurfaces.
The 'ended early' interrupted-session policy needs careful implementation across three consumers (Watch, Catalyst, History) to avoid the exact state-disagreement bug it's meant to prevent.
Discoverability of the Core ML-vs-heuristic disclosure is a design judgment call that could still end up too subtle in an actual build pass without explicit UI review.

Four-state Home surface adds design/implementation surface area versus a simpler three-state model, which must not be allowed to crowd out time needed for the core rep-counting/form-flagging algorithm work.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The product brief locks Formcheck's target user as a solo, privacy-motivated bodyweight trainee (squat/push-up/plank) who wants an honest rep count and one real geometric form correction without an account or cloud service. The core loop is confirmed as capability-check -> camera-placement guidance -> capture-or-demo-fixture -> on-device classification -> debounced geometric rule evaluation -> rep count + at most one named-joint form flag -> deterministic session finalization -> SwiftData persistence -> visibility across History/Charts/Watch/Catalyst. The phase resolved one real tension between the two takes: Codex initially proposed gating a 'stricter geometry engine with confidence scoring' and calibration profiles behind a paid tier, but this was rejected in favor of keeping the entire core loop -- rep counting and form-flagging fidelity for all three exercises, plus the demo session -- free and identical for all users forever, since gating core accuracy would contradict the already-locked sacrifice order (core loop never cut) and turn the free tier into an unconvincing demo. Formcheck Pro instead monetizes downstream depth and utility: unlimited session history, full per-exercise Swift Charts trend depth, Mac Catalyst frame-by-frame review with skeleton overlay, the HealthKit write, and full local data export. Three further decisions were locked: StoreKit 2's purchase/entitlement-refresh network calls to Apple are an explicit, narrow exception to the no-network rule (distinct from this app running its own backend), with cached entitlement honored offline indefinitely and never revoked mid-session; the app's only growth mechanic is a locally rendered, share-sheet-only summary card that can never include the underlying camera clip or frame, with no social feed or leaderboard; and cloud sync is explicitly out of scope for v1, with only a schema-level note that SwiftData should be structured to allow an optional future opt-in iCloud sync layer without a model rewrite. The competitive wedge (local explainability plus verifiable, honest capability-gap reporting) and the permanence of local-first behavior for both free and paid users were reconfirmed by both takes without disagreement.
open_risks: If a future build phase blurs the line between 'core loop' and 'paid depth features,' e.g. by quietly limiting free-tier form-flag detail, it would violate DEC-per_app_product_brief-001 and needs explicit review to prevent.

The share-card generation path must be implemented so it is structurally incapable of embedding clip/frame data, not just defaulted that way in UI, or the privacy guarantee central to the growth strategy could be silently broken.

StoreKit 2 entitlement caching logic (offline-indefinite, refresh-only-infrequently, never mid-session) is a nontrivial implementation detail that could be gotten wrong in a way that either breaks offline use or lets entitlement be gamed.

No paid-tier UX/paywall placement has been designed yet -- this brief sets the boundary of what's paid, not how or where the upsell is surfaced, which a later design phase must still resolve without pressuring the free core loop.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase locked the smallest valuable slice for Formcheck's build: implement the squat exercise through the complete, real pipeline end to end — capability check, camera-placement guidance, debounced live-capture state machine, one named geometric rule (hip-knee-ankle angle for depth), rep counting with felt per-rep feedback, a specific anatomically-worded form flag, deterministic session finalization, SwiftData persistence, and immediate visibility in History and its Swift Charts trend — with the demo-session fixture walking this identical path rather than existing as a separate mocked screen, since it's the only fully verifiable chain without real hardware. Build sequencing explicitly puts this slice before any Watch, Catalyst, HealthKit, or StoreKit/Pro work, reading the already-locked cut order (Catalyst, Watch, HealthKit before core loop) forward as a build priority rather than only a fallback cut list; those features and full export/erase are deferred (not abandoned), with Settings shipping minimally at first (exercise toggles plus the classification-method disclosure only, since that's cheap and required for honesty immediately). Concrete validation criteria were set: the demo toggle must produce a persisted, rule-flagged session visible in History/Charts in one sitting; the camera capability-blocked state must actually fire and be inspectable in Simulator, not just asserted; an interrupted session must resolve to exactly one consistent 'ended early' state; and the squat rule must be discoverable in-app within two taps. A explicit anti-shortcut decision was added: once squat proves the pipeline, push-up and plank must each get independently implemented and validated geometric rules rather than a copy-paste of squat's angle math onto different joints. Codex's CLI was unavailable this round, so this phase reflects a single synthesized take rather than a negotiated two-party convergence; there was no actual disagreement to resolve as a result.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex was unavailable), so this plan hasn't had the adversarial second-pass scrutiny earlier phases benefited from.
If push-up/plank rule validation is rushed once squat 'proves the concept,' the anti-copy-paste decision could still be honored in spirit but not in practice under time pressure.
The felt per-rep feedback requirement (haptic-like or visual pulse) needs concrete design specification in the build phase; this phase named the requirement but not its exact implementation.

Minimal Settings (toggle + disclosure only) must not become the permanent scope by default — HealthKit status, re-request, export, and erase are still contractually required and must resurface in a later phase, not be quietly forgotten because this slice deferred them.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Detailed discussion resolved seven concrete architecture/edge-case gaps left open by earlier phases, based on a single synthesized pass (Codex was unavailable this round). Crash/force-quit/thermal-kill interruptions were identified as a hole in the existing 'auto-finalize on interruption' decision, since those paths skip normal finalize code; the fix is incremental persistence of rep count/elapsed time plus a launch-time reconciliation scan that retroactively finalizes any orphaned in-progress session as 'ended early.' Plank was recognized as fundamentally incompatible with a repCount-primary session model since it's a continuous hold rather than a repeating motion, so hold-based exercises get their own metric shape (duration plus cumulative out-of-form seconds/instances) from the initial schema design. App Groups was named specifically (not just generically) as the likely entitlement wall for the shared cross-target SwiftData store, with a decided fallback: if blocked, the Watch app keeps no persistent store of its own and only mirrors transient state pushed live via WatchConnectivity. Camera-unavailable detection must distinguish three honest states (no hardware, access denied, access restricted) rather than collapsing them into one generic message. HealthKit writes are scoped down to duration and type only for v1, explicitly omitting any energy/calorie estimate rather than fabricating one from an assumed body mass, since a defensible MET-based estimate would require an additional read-permission scope not yet planned. Demo-fixture fencing must be enforced through a single reusable isDemo predicate applied at the persistence/query layer across Charts, HealthKit eligibility, and export, rather than per-screen UI checks that could be missed on a future addition. Finally, recorded clips must live in a backup-excluded private container, full erase must delete the actual clip files (not just database rows), and a failed/partial clip write under low disk space must never destroy the rest of a session's saved data.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex was unavailable again), so these resolutions haven't had adversarial second-pass scrutiny.
The plank hold-based metric shape adds a second session-model shape to design and implement correctly alongside the rep-based one, which is real added schema/UI surface area.

The App Groups fallback (Watch with no persistent store, message-passing only) needs to actually be validated against real project capability setup once build begins — it remains an assumption until then.

Incremental per-rep persistence plus launch-time reconciliation is nontrivial to implement correctly and must be tested against actual force-quit/crash scenarios, not just assumed to work from the design.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase locked Formcheck's MoSCoW feature tiering. Must-have is defined as one coherent unit — the full three-exercise capture-to-display loop plus the honesty layer that makes it trustworthy: a four-state Home/capture screen (empty, capability-blocked with three distinct honest camera-unavailable sub-states, ready, in-session); independently implemented and validated geometric rules for squat (hip-knee-ankle depth), push-up (elbow angle), and plank (hold-based duration + out-of-form-seconds, not repCount) each with debounce/hysteresis and a specific anatomically-worded form flag; a disclosed Core ML-or-heuristic exercise classifier; camera placement guidance; SwiftData persistence with incremental per-rep/per-second writes and launch-time reconciliation of orphaned in-progress sessions into 'ended early'; permanently non-editable rep counts; History plus per-exercise Swift Charts; a demo-session fixture walking the identical real pipeline and fenced via a shared isDemo predicate; exercise enable/disable in Settings; and a persistent, timestamped Known Limits screen. HealthKit write, the Watch companion, and Mac Catalyst review were explicitly placed in should-have (not must-have) and ranked in that order for acceptance priority, reasoning that the already-locked Catalyst-then-Watch-then-HealthKit sacrifice order only makes sense if none of the three is truly must-have — each gets a required, dated Known Limits fallback entry if not reached by build end, so demoting them doesn't quietly become abandoning them. Could-have covers StoreKit/Pro paywall, full export/erase, HealthKit re-request polish, and the share-sheet summary card. A hard won't-build list was locked: no exercises beyond the three, no manual rep editing, no cloud/social/accounts, no invented biometric numbers, no interval builders, no faked Simulator camera/Watch behavior under any circumstance, and no paid-tier accuracy advantage over free. A 32-item requirements-json was produced as the machine contract the build will be graded against, with core:true marking must-have items and core:false marking should/could items, and a decision was made that every requirement (including plank's, kept separate from squat/push-up's) must carry its own verification-method tag at build/review time rather than a narrative footnote. Codex was unavailable again this round, so this is a single synthesized take rather than a two-party negotiation, though it directly operationalizes prior phases' locked sacrifice order rather than introducing new tension.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex unavailable again), so the MoSCoW split hasn't had adversarial scrutiny from a second perspective.
The should-have fallback mechanism (dated Known Limits entry if untouched) depends on build-phase discipline to actually check and log it, not just a rule stated here.

32 requirements is a large surface for a single build cycle; if time runs short, the risk is must-have items 1-21 competing with each other for attention rather than the should-have tier absorbing the pressure as intended.

Plank's distinct acceptance criteria (hold-based, not rep-based) must actually be tested separately in QA/build phases, not folded into a generic 'rep counting works' check despite this phase's explicit decision against that.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Design discussion named Formcheck's design language as 'the quiet spotter' (a training partner watching from just behind your shoulder, speaking up only when something's wrong), with the emotional target of feeling watched-over and taken seriously rather than gamified. The signature interaction is the rep-completion moment: a dominant tabular-numeral counter with a physical pulse/haptic per rep, and a ~2-second amber joint/angle-tracing annotation with exact rule wording whenever a geometric form rule fires, with amber reserved exclusively for that purpose everywhere in the app. The default undesigned version of the app (stock TabView, plain camera preview, corner rep label, plain List history, buried About-page limitations) was explicitly rejected in favor of five concrete differences: dominant rep tally, single-purpose amber signal, tabular numerals throughout, Known Limits as a first-class nav destination, and persistently visually-fenced demo sessions (dashed border + badge) in both History rows and Session Detail. Home/Capture was specified as five states (empty/first-run, three-way capability-blocked, ready-to-record with a silhouette-alignment placement-guidance mechanic, in-session with a tappable classifier-override chip, and a visible finalizing state), closing a previously-unaddressed gap where a misdetected exercise would silently run the wrong geometric rule for an entire set. A Post-Set Summary sheet (reusing Session Detail content, not a new screen) was added to close the session-ending moment before landing in History. Settings was locked to never show a live-looking control for an unfinished should-have feature, routing instead to a dated Known Limits explanation, consistent with the already-locked should-have fallback rule. Accessibility was elevated to core given that push-up and plank both put the user's face toward the floor during the exact moment the app's value fires: an optional audio cue alongside the per-rep/per-flag haptic, explicit VoiceOver announcements on each rep and flag, Dynamic Type support for the hero counter, and icon+text (never color-only) capability-blocked states. Codex was unavailable again this round, so this is a single synthesized design take rather than a two-party negotiation.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex unavailable again), so the design system hasn't had adversarial scrutiny from a second design perspective.

The silhouette-alignment placement-guidance mechanic is specified as a concept but not yet as concrete geometry/thresholds — a later build phase must define exactly how alignment is measured and when Start enables.

The Post-Set Summary sheet and classifier-override chip are both real, if modest, additions to build scope layered on top of an already-large must-have list; they must not be allowed to consume time earmarked for the three independently-validated exercise geometric rules.

Audio-cue-on-form-flag and full VoiceOver rep/flag announcements are now specified as must-have accessibility behavior, which adds implementation surface that must be planned for from the start of the build, not retrofitted.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Design handoff produced Formcheck's complete build-ready design spec, structured around one core architectural decision: Home/Capture is a full-screen modal owning a single CaptureSessionModel that is the sole writer to SwiftData and WatchConnectivity, with History, Charts, Session Detail, and the Watch app as pure readers — this prevents the tab bar from creating a state where a mid-set navigation either silently drops the set or leaves the camera running invisibly, the exact cross-surface-disagreement failure mode priority (c) forbids. The modal independently re-checks capability on appear rather than trusting Home's precomputed state, closing a race where camera access changes between the two. The spec fully specifies: a type scale with a custom non-default Dynamic Type rule for the RepHero counter (large base size, minimumScaleFactor, vertically-growing container); an 8pt spacing grid; light/dark hex values for every color role, including a two-token amber system (amberStroke for graphics, amberText for rule-wording text) needed because one shared amber value can't satisfy both the 3:1 graphical and 4.5:1 text contrast thresholds; four named corner-radius steps; a full component inventory mapped to every screen across iPhone, Watch, and Catalyst; the complete navigation map (iPhone TabView with capture as fullScreenCover and Post-Set Summary as an auto-snapping sheet, Watch's two-screen idle/in-session stack, Catalyst's standalone NavigationSplitView with zero capture UI); per-screen empty/loading/populated/error states including three distinct capability-blocked sub-states and Settings rows that route unfinished should-have features to Known Limits instead of showing a dead control; precise motion/haptic timing including a Reduce-Motion path that degrades animation but preserves the amber annotation's full informational hold duration; and an accessibility section requiring explicit AccessibilityNotification.Announcement posts for rep/flag VoiceOver events rather than label-diffing, since the capture view is a largely non-interactive full-screen camera surface. The phase explicitly decided against routing to external Claude Design, since every token needed to write Theme.swift directly is already specified with no invented values, reserving external design only as a future option for marketing assets outside the app itself. Codex was unavailable again this round, so this is a single synthesized take, though it directly operationalizes every prior design_discussion and detailed_discussion decision rather than introducing new unresolved tension.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex unavailable again), so the spec hasn't had adversarial scrutiny from a second design/engineering perspective.

The redundant capability re-check in the capture modal is specified as a requirement but its exact implementation (polling vs. reactive AVCaptureDevice authorization observation) is left to the build phase.

The two-token amber system and the non-standard RepHero Dynamic Type rule are both easy to get subtly wrong in implementation (e.g. reusing amberStroke where amberText belongs, or clipping the hero counter at largest accessibility sizes) and should be specifically checked during build QA.

The component inventory and per-screen state list are large; if build time is tight, the risk is these being implemented shallowly (e.g. missing the Reduce-Motion branch) rather than dropped outright, which could look done without actually meeting the spec.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The iOS architecture review locked Formcheck's implementation-level architecture ahead of tech_specs, driven by a single synthesized Claude pass (Codex unavailable again). The most consequential correction: the 'one shared SwiftData store across iOS/watchOS/Catalyst' framing from portfolio_selection is physically impossible for Catalyst, since a Mac and an iPhone cannot share a local store without iCloud sync or a network call, both banned — the fix is giving Catalyst its own local store on the same schema, populated only via user-initiated export/import (AirDrop/Files/cable), which makes Catalyst's usefulness for real sessions newly dependent on the export feature shipping. A related gap was closed: the demo fixture needs a bundled placeholder video clip, not just synthetic pose data, or Catalyst's frame-by-frame review has nothing to open. The capture pipeline is specified concretely: per-frame Vision processing off the AVCaptureVideoDataOutput queue with late-frame discarding (never queuing backlog), and AVCaptureSession interruptions (calls, Control Center recording, another app grabbing the camera) now route into the same 'ended early' finalize path as backgrounding/crash. A JointFrame value-type abstraction decouples rule/classifier logic from raw Vision types, making the exercise rules independently unit-testable and letting the demo fixture and live capture share one real pipeline. SwiftData schema is locked as one flat WorkoutSession model (ExerciseKind enum, both rep- and hold-based metric fields, incremental-persistence and sessionStatus fields) written via a background ModelActor, explicitly avoiding SwiftData class inheritance. Permissions are minimized and justified: video-only capture with no microphone permission at all, HealthKit write-only scope, no Photos permission anywhere. HealthKit's entitlement risk is upgraded from 'unconfirmed' to 'assume blocked until proven otherwise' with a pre-written Known Limits fallback, while StoreKit 2 is downgraded from requires-real-hardware to Simulator-verified since local .storekit config files support full purchase/refund/renewal testing without a sandbox account. WCSession is wrapped in a small protocol enabling genuine Simulator-run unit tests of the Watch-unreachable path. A five-bucket testing strategy was locked spanning fixture-driven rule-engine tests, in-memory persistence/reconciliation tests, XCUITest capability-blocked coverage, WCSession fake-relay tests, and Simulator StoreKit tests, leaving only live camera accuracy, real Watch pairing/haptics, and Catalyst signing/window behavior as genuinely hardware-only.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped this phase (Codex unavailable again), so the architecture hasn't had adversarial scrutiny from a second engineering perspective.

Catalyst's real-session usefulness is now explicitly coupled to the export/import feature (currently could-have) actually shipping — if export is cut under time pressure, Catalyst becomes permanently demo-only, which is a bigger consequence than 'Catalyst polish, cut first' implied earlier.

The JointFrame adapter and background ModelActor are both real, non-trivial pieces of infrastructure that need to exist before any exercise rule work can be properly unit-tested — they must be built early, not retrofitted.

The assumption that HealthKit is blocked without a paid developer account is itself unverified until actual project/capability setup is attempted; it's now a stated architectural assumption rather than an open question, which could still turn out wrong in either direction.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Tech specs locked Formcheck's build-ready technical architecture in a single synthesized Claude pass (Codex unavailable all rounds). Module layout is one local Swift package, FormcheckCore (models, JointFrame pose adapter, rule engines, classifier, persistence actor, fixtures, Known Limits, export/import, WatchRelay protocol), consumed by two build products: Formcheck (the iOS app target with Mac Catalyst enabled as a destination on the same target, not a separate fourth Xcode target, correcting earlier phrasing) and FormcheckWatch. The three exercise geometric rules were given concrete, checkable numbers for the first time: squat uses hip-knee-ankle knee angle (standing >160 deg, depth <100 deg), push-up uses shoulder-elbow-wrist elbow angle (standing >160 deg, depth <90 deg), and plank uses shoulder-hip-ankle hip angle (180 deg target, 15 deg tolerance, 1s sustained-deviation window before accruing outOfFormSeconds), all sharing one RepStateMachine hysteresis/debounce primitive; every failed-depth rep still counts but fires a flag naming the actual measured angle, never generic text. Exercise classification is locked as an explainable heuristic (torso orientation plus joint-cyclicity variance over a rolling window), explicitly not a Core ML model, since no labeled training data exists for this project — a documented, justified choice rather than an ambiguous placeholder. Two previously-unaddressed edge cases were closed: multi-person-in-frame handling (select the largest-bounding-box pose observation, tie-broken by confidence, ignore the rest) and a crash-during-finalizing race (a new SessionStatus.finalizing case set synchronously the instant End is tapped, so a crash in that window reconciles identically to a mid-session crash rather than being misread as a clean completion or lost entirely). A complete interfaces-json type contract covering every cross-lane model, protocol, service, and view was produced for parallel build lanes to code against directly. Persistence and the five-bucket testing strategy carry forward unchanged from ios_architecture_review, now backed by concrete fixture data shared identically between unit tests and the demo-fixture path.
open_risks: Only one contributor's take shaped every round of this phase (Codex unavailable throughout), so the architecture and the geometric thresholds haven't had adversarial scrutiny from a second engineering perspective.

The Catalyst-as-destination-not-separate-target decision is a real deviation from how earlier phases described 'Mac Catalyst target' — later phases and build lanes must pick up this correction rather than assuming a literal fourth Xcode target.

The specific angle thresholds (160/100 for squat, 160/90 for push-up, 180±15 for plank) are engineering estimates, not validated against real human movement data or a labeled dataset; if they prove miscalibrated against real camera captures, that itself needs to surface as a Known Limits entry rather than being silently adjusted without disclosure.

The .finalizing status transition and multi-person observation-selection rule are both new, non-trivial pieces of logic that need explicit unit test coverage in the build phase, not just design-level intent.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The project plan for Formcheck locked a strict, gated milestone sequence built on top of tech_specs' interfaces-json, produced from a single Claude systems-engineer pass (Codex unavailable). Milestone 0 is the FormcheckCore skeleton (models, JointFrame adapter, RepStateMachine, all three rule engines, classifier, SessionRepository, reconciliation, Known Limits) built and fixture-tested in complete isolation, blocking all UI/Watch/Catalyst work until its test bucket passes -- this milestone also picked up two newly-identified tasks: an explicit metric-shape consistency check in SessionRepository.finalize() (preventing a squat session from carrying holdDuration or vice versa, a representable-invalid-state corruption path no prior phase caught) and a concrete low-disk-space partial-clip-write unit test. A Milestone 0.5 spike was added to verify SwiftData's background-ModelActor-to-main-context-@Query propagation actually works promptly before building History/Charts on top of an unverified assumption, with a budgeted fallback (an explicit refresh signal) if it doesn't. summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This round scoped the fix for the persistently-failing 'Demo session end-to-end' UI-crawl flow, which now fails one step earlier than before (home.startSetButton not found at all, not even listed among the crawler's discovered controls — only tab labels show). The working theory is that HomeView.swift gates its entire demoControls section (Start Set, live rep/elapsed display, End/Complete, and the flow's other missing elements) behind `if let phase = captureModel?.phase`, and captureModel is only constructed inside .onAppear, creating a render race where the crawler's snapshot can occur before the lazy init completes, making the whole block invisible rather than just mis-labeled. The group declined to jump straight to a code fix, instead scoping a diagnostic-first approach: first confirm CaptureSessionModel's initializer has no side effects (HealthKit prompts, WatchConnectivity activation) before deciding whether to move its construction eagerly into a non-optional @State/@StateObject (safe if side-effect-free) or instead restructure only HomeView's render gate to show the demoControls scaffold unconditionally while CaptureSessionModel's construction stays deferred (required if side effects exist). Either path stays within HomeView's rendering/state-initialization layer, with CaptureSessionModel's finalization logic, rule engines, classifier, persistence, Package.swift, any .pbxproj, Info.plist, and entitlements files remaining forbidden-edit zones. Done is defined as a temporary observable marker proving readiness on first paint plus an actual UI-crawl tool run observed passing the flow past the startSetButton step — not another round of compile-only or source-read verification, which this project's history shows has been wrong before (the tab-bar identifier saga took two incorrect rounds before landing on the real SwiftUI/XCUITest hit-testing cause). This round's eventual fix, regardless of outcome, does not soften the app's standing no-go verdict or launch blockers.
open_risks: The timing hypothesis (captureModel nil until onAppear hiding the whole demoControls block) is still unconfirmed against real crawler behavior — it could instead be that the crawler fails on an earlier step and never reaches a fully-rendered Home at all, which would make an eager-init fix ineffective
